output: Self-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence [c2]. It has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [c2, 4, 27, 28, 22].

The Transformer uses the "Scaled Dot-Product Attention" [c8] and "Multi-Head Attention" [c10] attention functions. The Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and then project the results h times with different, learned linear projections to dk dimensions, resulting in dv-dimensional output values [c10]. The Multi-Head Attention [c10] combines the output of h attention heads, each of which computes the Scaled Dot-Product Attention, and concatenates the results with a weight matrix W O [c10].
The dot products are scaled by √dk to prevent the softmax function from being pushed into regions where it has extremely small gradients, which can lead to unstable optimization [c4].

The base Transformer has 6 identical layers in both the encoder and the decoder [c8]. Each layer in the encoder and decoder contains two sub-layers: a multi-head self-attention mechanism and a simple, position-wise fully connected feed-forward network [c9].
The model dimension is 512 [c6] and the number of attention heads is 8 [c6].

Multi-head attention is a technique that allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions [c7]. It is used in the Transformer model to perform self-attention, where the queries, keys, and values are projected to different dimensions, and the attention function is applied in parallel across multiple heads [c7]. This allows the model to capture long-range dependencies and relationships between different parts of the input [c10].

The Transformer gives the model information about the order of tokens through "positional encodings" added to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks [c6]. These positional encodings have the same dimension as the embeddings, so that the model can make use of the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

The authors used the Adam optimizer [20] with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98 and ϵ = 10−9. The learning rate varied over the course of training, according to the formula: lrate = d−0.5 model · min(step_num−0.5, step_num · warmup_steps−1.5) [c8].
The paper employs three types of regularization: dropout [20], the sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer [33], and positional embedding [c7].
The big Transformer achieved a BLEU score of 28.4 on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task and a BLEU score of 41.0 on the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task [c5].

The paper argues that self-attention is preferable to recurrent and convolutional layers because it allows for more parallelization of computations, reducing the total computational complexity per layer, and enables the model to learn long-range dependencies more efficiently, as it can attend over all positions in the input sequence [c4].

The purpose of masking in the decoder's self-attention is to prevent leftward information flow, ensuring that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i. This is achieved by masking out (setting to −∞) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections [c5].
